title: Verifier-Gated LLM NetOps: A Preregistered Artifact-Backed Evaluation of Input Sanitization and Deterministic Verification
abstract: We report a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment (study_id cand-2026-03) that measured whether template-based input sanitization combined with deterministic verifier-gating (and at-most-one automated repair) changes the rate at which a deterministic validator accepts LLM-generated CLI configurations under adversarially mutated intents. The frozen run used the declared generator gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 within an orchestration adapter. Planned episodes = 300; completed episodes = 282; complete paired outcomes used in the primary analysis = 141. Observed per-pair acceptance: Baseline 135/141 (95.7447%); Guarded 141/141 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.04255319148936165; exact two-sided McNemar p = 0.03125; 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]. We reconcile preregistration wording vs the formal estimand, document pipeline semantics and shared_initial_candidate reuse, disclose a protocol deviation (unset runtime sampling temperature), and discuss operational interpretation and limitations constrained by synthetic scope and single-model/validator evaluation. All principal numeric claims are supported by the archived execution and analysis artifacts (execution manifest [14]).

sections.introduction:
Automating NetOps tasks with large language models (LLMs) can reduce manual effort by translating operator intent to device CLI, but operational deployment requires strong safety guarantees: generated sequences must respect ordering constraints, device-specific grammar, and explicit safety invariants. Deterministic validators — tools that check explicit configuration invariants and report property-level violations — are a natural deployment gate for LLM-assisted NetOps because they evaluate semantics relevant to deployability rather than surface similarity. However, the practical efficacy of combining template-based input sanitization, verifier-gating, and bounded automated repair in the presence of adversarially mutated intents has not been measured under a preregistered paired design that isolates downstream pipeline effects.

This paper answers a narrowly scoped, preregistered question: for a synthetic adversarial intent bank, does combining template-based sanitization with deterministic verifier-gating (plus at-most-one automated repair) change the probability that a deterministic validator accepts an LLM-generated configuration when the generation call is shared across conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics)? We executed the preregistered study cand-2026-03 end-to-end, reconciled preregistration language with the formal estimand, and report confirmatory paired inference using an exact two-sided McNemar test together with paired bootstrap confidence intervals. Our execution artifacts, per-episode validator traces, and statistical analysis are archived and cited in the execution manifest [14].
sections.related_work:
Deterministic verification and validator-centered evaluation are long-standing practices in networking: Header Space Analysis, NetPlumber-style approaches, and VeriFlow operationalize property-level checks (reachability, isolation, ordering) that are directly relevant to deployability and safety [5–7]. Empirical evaluations of LLMs for configuration generation (e.g., NetConfEval, NetLLMBench) consistently report that model-only generation produces syntactic and higher-level semantic mistakes (ordering, precondition violations) and that string-match metrics correlate poorly with deployability [3,8,9]. The security literature documents prompt-injection and indirect prompt attacks that can subvert agentic pipelines when external text is not sanitized or when downstream checks are insufficiently strict [10, 33].

Generate–validate–repair architectures that couple generation with verifier diagnostics and constrained repair have been proposed and shown in prototypes to reduce observable errors when verifier feedback is precise and repairs are bounded [11, 37]. Despite these demonstrations, prior work leaves open practical questions about (a) how much repair-and-gating changes validator acceptance under adversarial inputs, (b) how to quantify operational tradeoffs (reduced rework vs potential masking of adversarial manipulations), and (c) how to design paired experiments that isolate post-generation pipeline effects. Our study situates itself in this gap by preregistering a paired estimand based on deterministic-validator acceptance and by executing the design under shared_initial_candidate semantics so that any observed paired difference can only arise from downstream sanitization, gating, and permitted repair.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study cand-2026-03 was preregistered prior to observing outcomes (preregistration archived; see execution manifest [14]). The primary formal estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: for each adversarial intent the binary outcome equals 1 if the deterministic validator accepts the pipeline-final candidate for deployment and 0 otherwise. The preregistered confirmatory test is the exact two-sided McNemar on paired outcomes; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs use 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729).

Design, tasks, and adversary model. The planned confirmatory scenario specified N = 150 adversarial intent templates, yielding 300 planned runs across two conditions (Baseline and Guarded). Intent templates exercise interface admin changes, MTU and VLAN updates, sequencing constraints (shutdown–change–restore patterns), and protected-interface rules. An adversary model applied deterministic mutation heuristics to templates; task-generation seeds and mutation taxonomy are archived in the manifest [14]. Scope is explicitly synthetic and limited to the encoded CLI grammar and validator semantics; no production traffic was used.

Model, validator, and orchestration. Declared components were generator = gpt-5-mini and validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, orchestrated by a hosted generate–validate–repair adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1). The guarded pipeline applied template-based input sanitization, then deterministically gated candidates failing explicit checks; when the guarded policy permitted it, the pipeline allowed at-most-one automated repair LLM call. The archived model configuration records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and an unset sampling temperature (temperature = null), which we disclose as a protocol deviation (see Disclosure Statement). To preserve comparability despite the unset parameter the run used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial generation per intent reused by both conditions) so that any paired difference arises only from sanitizer/gating/repair and final validation.

Execution, missingness, and analysis plan. Planned episodes = 300. The preregistered missingness rule excluded a paired unit only when both paired runs were technical failures. The archive reports completed_episodes = 282 and failed_episodes = 18; after applying the preregistered exclusion rule 141 complete pairs entered the primary analysis. Primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 (exact McNemar) and paired bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). A conservative sensitivity check treating excluded both-missing pairs as failures is reported in Results.
sections.results:
Execution summary and counts. The run completed 282 of 300 planned episodes; 18 episodes failed technically and were handled per preregistered rules. After exclusions 141 complete paired units were analyzed. Provider-call accounting recorded 156 hosted model-call events (147 completed, 9 failed); stage counts show 150 shared_initial_generation events and 6 repair-stage events (reconciliation artifacts cited in [14]).

Condition-level acceptance and paired contingency. Condition summaries for the 141 analyzed pairs: Baseline successes = 135/141 (baseline success rate = 0.9574468085106383); Guarded successes = 141/141 (guarded success rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table entries used in inference were n11 = 135 (both accepted), n10 = 6 (guarded accepted, baseline rejected), n01 = 0 (baseline accepted, guarded rejected), n00 = 0 (both rejected).

Inferential results. The preregistered confirmatory exact two-sided McNemar test yields p = 0.03125. The paired point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.04255319148936165. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]. All numbers and test parameters are archived and reproducible from the analysis artifacts in the execution manifest [14].

Discordant-case diagnostics and repair association. The six discordant (n10) pairs are traceable in per-episode validator traces: each of these pairs shows sanitizer normalization and/or a single permitted automated repair that converted a draft rejected by the baseline validator into a final candidate accepted by the guarded pipeline. The reconciliation artifact reports repair-stage count = 6 and links each discordant pair to one repair event; archived per-episode traces provide detailed diagnostics (see execution manifest [14]).

Sensitivity to technical-failure exclusions. Nine paired units were excluded because both runs failed technically. As a conservative sensitivity check (not the preregistered primary analysis), treating the nine excluded pairs as failures yields baseline acceptance = 135/150 = 0.9000 and guarded acceptance = 141/150 = 0.9400. This sensitivity illustrates that technical failures reduce effective sample size but do not reverse the observed paired direction under this conservative assumption.

Unexecuted preregistered items. The preregistered benign-control (M = 50) and the false-positive-blocking secondary estimand were not executed; therefore no empirical false-positive-blocking rates are reported here. This omission is documented in the preregistration and execution manifest [14].
sections.discussion:
Interpretation relative to the formal estimand. The preregistered formal estimand measured paired validator acceptance-for-deployment (guarded − baseline) under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The observed guarded→higher acceptance (≈4.255 percentage points) therefore indicates that sanitizer plus bounded repair recovered drafts that the validator would otherwise reject; it does not by itself imply a reduction in attacker success under an attacker-centric definition. A repair that converts malformed but benign drafts into validator-accepted candidates is operationally useful (reduced operator rework) but could be harmful if repairs mask adversarial manipulations — distinguishing these outcomes requires an independent semantic-safety oracle not present in the current run.

Statistical and practical considerations. The absolute effect is modest against a high baseline (ceiling effect): moving from ≈95.7% to 100% acceptance yields statistical detectability (p = 0.03125) and a paired bootstrap CI excluding zero, but the practical impact depends on the operational baseline error rate and the semantic fidelity of repairs. The preregistered power target assumed a larger detectable effect (≈20 percentage points); the achieved discordant counts (n10 = 6, n01 = 0) produce a smaller observed estimate with narrower uncertainty than a worst-case small-sample bound would suggest because all discordant counts are one-sided in direction.

Operational implications and co-design. In synthetic settings where validator coverage matches the intended invariants, sanitizer+bounded-repair can lower manual rework by recovering reparable drafts. However, deployment requires co-design: gating policies, repair scope, and validator expressiveness must be jointly specified and audited. Repairs should be constrained to semantics-preserving edits and coupled with provenance/traceability so operators can inspect repaired changes before deployment.

Threats to validity and generalizability. Construct validity: deterministic validator coverage is partial (CLI grammar, required sequences, protected-interface rules) and does not capture all protocol- or runtime-level semantics; acceptance-for-deployment is therefore a partial proxy for operational safety. External validity: evaluation used one generator (gpt-5-mini), one validator implementation, and a synthetic intent bank; results may not generalize to different models, vendors, CLI dialects, or production traffic. Internal validity: technical failures (18/300) reduced effective pairs; exclusions followed the preregistered rule. The protocol deviation (unset sampling temperature) introduces uncontrolled provider-side sampling behavior; the shared_initial_candidate design preserves within-pair comparability but explicit deterministic reproduction requires setting temperature = 0 and re-executing (recommendation described in Methodology and archived manifest [14]).

Recommendations. (1) Execute the preregistered benign-control to measure false-positive blocking; (2) preregister and measure attacker-centric estimands that combine validator acceptance with an independent semantic-safety oracle or reachability tests; (3) diversify generators and validators across vendors and CLI dialects; (4) fix sampling settings (temperature = 0) for deterministic reproduction; and (5) restrict automatic repairs to narrowly scoped, semantics-preserving edits with operator-reviewed audit trails. Each recommendation follows directly from the archived evidence and provider-call accounting (execution manifest [14]).
sections.conclusion: A preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment on a synthetic adversarial intent bank found that template-based input sanitization combined with deterministic verifier-gating and at-most-one automated repair produced a small but statistically detectable absolute increase in deterministic-validator-accepted LLM-generated configurations under the archived formal estimand (paired difference = 0.04255319148936165; p = 0.03125; 95% CI [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]). Diagnostics link the six discordant pairs to single permitted repairs that enabled acceptance. Crucially, improved validator acceptance under this estimand does not substitute for an attacker-centric safety demonstration; measuring reductions in attacker success requires an independent semantic-safety oracle and broader evaluation across models, validators, and real-world datasets. All principal numeric claims and reconciliation statements above are supported by archived execution and analysis artifacts; the execution manifest is the primary machine-verifiable archive and is cited as [14].

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock under the archived master prompt (provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA-256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: a human Research Director selected the topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; all literature review, preregistration, study selection, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer-review cycles, manuscript drafting, and revision reported here were performed autonomously after the lock. Declared models/tools and orchestration: primary generator = gpt-5-mini; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; orchestration adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration: study cand-2026-03 was preregistered and archived prior to observing outcomes (preregistration archived; see execution manifest [14]). Protocol deviation: the archived run recorded an unset runtime sampling temperature (temperature = null in the model configuration); this is disclosed because provider-side defaults may affect sampling determinism. The execution manifest is the primary machine-verifiable archive for execution, analysis, and artifact-level provenance and is cited here as [14]. No human manually edited or corrected the manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Synthetic task bank and intent templates — not real production traffic or operator logs; results may not generalize to field datasets.
Single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) and single validator implementation limit external validity across vendors, protocols, and model families.
Validator coverage constrained to encoded safety properties (CLI grammar, required sequences, protected-interface invariants); some protocol-level or dynamic runtime semantics are not represented.
Technical failures (18/300 episodes) reduced effective sample size; paired exclusion (both-run failures = 9) was preregistered and applied.
Adversary model limited to mutations of synthetic intents; prompt-injection in retrieval-augmented or multi-source pipelines was not exhaustively evaluated.
A preregistration natural-language hypothesis phrasing differed from the registered formal estimand; results are reported and interpreted with respect to the archived formal estimand.
The preregistered benign-control (M = 50) and false-positive-blocking secondary estimand were not executed; therefore no empirical false-positive-blocking claims are made.
